process.quote: Where a marker suspects that academic misconduct has occurred, they will inform the Sub-Board using a Suspected Academic Misconduct form.

Where an allegation of an academic misconduct has been made and the case is being investigated, you will not be disadvantaged unless there is evidence to substantiate an allegation with an associated outcome.
You will be offered the opportunity to make representations to the Panel. This can be in writing and/or by attending the Panel and speaking in person.
If you contest the allegation, a Panel Meeting will take place.
If you do not respond within 10 working days without good reason, or decline the date offered, the Panel may decide the case in your absence.

You may choose to be accompanied by a companion, who should be a member of the College (for example a fellow student, member of staff, someone from the Student Union Advice team or a College-approved mentor).
You can appeal decisions made at any stage of this policy by submitting an appeal form, following the College’s Appeals Policy and Procedure.
You will be informed of the outcome applied in writing, within 10 working days.
The standard of proof required is that of a balance of probabilities.

definitions.quote: ‘Collusion’ means presenting work as your own that has been done in unauthorised partnership with someone else, where this is not permitted by the requirements of the assessment.
‘Contract cheating’, also known as ‘essay mills’, ‘ghost writers’ or ‘third-party cheating’, means submitting work as your own that has been purchased or commissioned from someone else.
‘Fabrication’ means creating false data or other aspects of research or assessed work.
‘Falsification’ means falsely claiming to have carried out part of an assessment, such as experiments, observations, interviews, or any form of research and/or
‘Impersonation’ means assuming the identity of another student, or allowing someone to assume your identity, in an assessment.
‘Plagiarism’ is when you present work as if it is your own, without full, accurate, and appropriate referencing.
‘Self-plagiarism’ involves submitting the same work for credit more than once, where this is not permitted by the requirements of the assessment.

‘Academic misconduct’ means a breach of academic integrity, through actions which could lead you to gain an unfair academic advantage in an assessment; for example, by taking credit for someone else’s work, words, or ideas.
